q: What are prefill and decode?
short: Prefill runs the full prompt through the model in parallel, filling the KV cache and producing the first token; decode then generates one token per step, attending to the cached keys and values.
detail: Prefill sets TTFT, decode sets TPOT.
mistakes: Thinking the prompt is processed token by token.

q: What is the KV cache?
short: Stored keys and values of all previous tokens for every layer, so each new token only computes its own K/V and attends to the cache instead of recomputing the whole prefix.
example: 0.5 MiB per token for a 7B-class model.

q: Greedy vs beam search?
short: Greedy takes the top token each step (fast, myopic). Beam search keeps the B best partial sequences, finding higher-likelihood outputs at B× the compute; good for translation, bland for open-ended text.
example: Greedy A z 0.24 vs beam B x 0.36.
follow: Why is beam bland for chat?
mistakes: Claiming greedy finds the most likely sequence.

q: Top-k vs top-p?
short: Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens; top-p keeps the smallest set whose probabilities sum to p, so it adapts to the model's confidence.

q: What does temperature do?
short: Divides logits by T before softmax: T < 1 sharpens toward the top token, T > 1 flattens toward uniform, T → 0 is greedy.

q: KV-cache size for 32 layers, width 4096, 16-bit, 2048 tokens?
short: 2 × 32 × 4096 × 2 = 524,288 bytes/token ≈ 0.5 MiB; × 2048 ≈ 1 GiB per sequence.
mistakes: Forgetting the factor 2 for K and V.

q: Why is decoding memory-bandwidth bound?
short: Each step reads every weight once but performs only ~2 FLOPs per parameter for a single token, so the GPU waits on memory reads rather than arithmetic.
mistakes: Buying more FLOPs to speed decode.

q: What is GQA?
short: Grouped-query attention: query heads are split into groups that each share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache (e.g. 32 → 8 KV heads, 4× smaller) with little quality loss.

q: Upper bound on tokens/s for a 13B fp16 model at 3 TB/s, batch 1?
short: Weights 26 GB; 26 / 3000 GB/s ≈ 8.7 ms per token → ≤ ~115 tokens/s.
follow: Effect of KV cache at long context?
mistakes: Using FLOPs to estimate decode speed.

q: Why does beam search produce dull text in open-ended generation?
short: Maximising likelihood favours generic, high-frequency continuations and repetition loops; human text is not the highest-probability text, so sampling with truncation reads more naturally.

q: Apply T = 2 to probabilities (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10).
short: Equivalent to taking square roots and renormalising: √ → 0.707, 0.5, 0.387, 0.316; sum 1.91 → 0.37, 0.26, 0.20, 0.17.

q: MQA vs GQA vs MLA?
short: MQA: one K/V head for all queries (largest saving, most quality risk). GQA: a few shared groups (balanced). MLA: cache a compressed latent and expand to per-head K/V (big saving, keeps head diversity, more compute).
mistakes: Thinking these change the query count.

q: How does batching change decode efficiency?
short: One weight read serves all sequences in the batch, so throughput rises nearly linearly until compute or KV-cache memory becomes the limit; per-user latency rises slightly.

q: Why not recompute K/V instead of caching?
short: Recomputing all previous tokens' keys and values at every step makes generation O(n²) in forward work; caching makes each step O(n) attention plus constant projection work, at the cost of memory.

q: Choose decoding settings for a code assistant and for a story writer.
short: Code: low temperature (0–0.2), greedy or small top-p, stop sequences, maybe multiple samples ranked by tests. Story: T ≈ 0.8–1.0, top-p 0.9–0.95, repetition penalty.

q: How many 8k-token sequences fit in 40 GB of cache with GQA (8 KV heads, 128 dims, 32 layers, 16-bit)?
short: Per token 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 B; per sequence × 8192 = 1 GiB; 40 GB / ~1.07 GB ≈ 37 sequences (vs ~9 with MHA).

q: How does long context change decode cost?
short: Each step also reads the whole KV cache, so per-token time grows with context; at long context, cache reads can exceed weight reads, making attention memory traffic the bottleneck.
detail: Hence GQA, MLA, cache quantization, windows.

q: What is speculative sampling's relation to decoding rules?
short: A draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass; an acceptance–rejection rule guarantees the output distribution equals the target's sampling distribution (M6).

q: Why can greedy decoding be non-deterministic in practice?
short: Floating-point reductions in different orders (batch composition, kernels, parallelism) can flip near-ties between top tokens, after which the sequences diverge.

q: Design a decoding stack for a chatbot under heavy load.
short: GQA model, 16-bit or 8-bit KV cache with paged allocation, continuous batching, top-p 0.9 with T 0.7, repetition penalty, max-length and stop sequences, speculative decoding for latency, and per-request limits on context.
follow: How would you measure quality impact?
